I'll take that, gimme a sec…

When you have an entire orchestra set up ready to combo out, and need an extra power to do so, badly enough to bleed for it, Polyphoric flare is the best card in Argent's deck.

When your allies want their best stuff back the turn after their next turn, Vernal Sonata is the best card in Argent's deck.  (The 1 HP is generally just gravy, save perhaps if Scholar is in the game.)

When 1 HP every turn isn't just gravy (or Scholar is in the game), Rhapsody of Vigor is the best card in Argent's deck.

When 2 HP every turn would be even more not-just-gravy, or when you want to do something resembling actual damage, possibly while getting a Blinding Speed effect (or two, if you give up the damage part) every turn, Drake's Pipes is the best card in Argent's deck.

When your teammates are a lot more helpful than you are, you can get multiple Accompanies a turn, you have original Nightmist , Omnitron-X, or The Scholar on your team, or you're playing a slower-rolling villain which you'll need long-term help defeating, Inventive Preparation is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you have a bonus to damage or are teamed up with Absolute Zero (I have to remember to try this!), Scherzo of Frost and Flame is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you don't have another instrument, Eydisiar's Horn is the best card in Argent's deck (assuming it's not your first turn and you didn't just get wiped).

When you don't have an Instrument, want to have another Instrument, or would like to increase your hand size, Instrumental Conjuration is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you feel like being weird and doing your Accompany first, Anpuku's Drum is the best card in Argent's deck.

When a lot of 1-damage instances are flying around, the highest or lowest HP hero is taking a lot of hits, Nightmist or some similar hero needs every card they can get, or you can get multiple Rhythm accompanies in a turn, Counterpoint Bulwark is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you have two different kinds of songs that are worth playing, neither of which is a Melody, Telamon's Lyra is the best card in Argent's deck.

When any of your teammates is doing a lot of little damage pings, and/or can boost little-damage pings into something significant, Syncopated Onslaught is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you need a versatile and reusable tool to solve a wide variety of situations that don't involve dealing damage, Sarabande of Destruction is the best card in Argent's deck.

When you want to be able to play any damn Accompany you want, Xu's Bell is the best card in Argent's deck.

When what you need is the best Instrument in Argent's deck, Musaragni's Harp is the best card in Argent's deck.  (This is particularly true on turn 2, when it and Xu's Bell are the only cards that will let you get both halves of whatever song you played on turn 1, unless you opened on Subdominant and another song, which might let you use the Drum or Horn effectively.  Of the two, the Bell is slightly less likely to be optimal, despite being apparently stronger, since Rhythm performs are weaker than Harmonies on average, though it will always depend on the situation.)

When THAT HAS TO DIE RIGHT NOW, or when you can get one or more Harmony-Accompanies and don't badly need to heal, Cedistic Dissonant is the best card in Argent's deck.

Whenever you have a non-Melody song in play, Silver Shadow is the best card in Argent's deck.  Even if you don't, it's pretty damn good.

When you need to play more cards in the early game, or combo out in the late game, Alacritous Subdominant is the best card in Argent's deck.

The rest of the time, Inspiring Supertonic is the best card in Argent's deck.  I mean, it gives you more powers to play all the other songs with, so it kind of can't help but be the very best in most situations.

At all times, Arcane Cadence is tied with the other best card in Argent's deck, since it gives you roughly a 1/2 to 1/4 chance of being that card, plus letting you draw another card and stack your deck a little.

posts.cooked:
Oh great... Both of them... Well this may take a bit...

Firstly, someone will most likely say "DR will hurt that, because DR always exist, bleh... bleh... bleh..." There are 7 heroes capable of increasing damage. There are also 5 environments that also increase all damage, also the Tomb of Anubis that can give a power that deals a base of 2 damage, making it 6 Environments that can help increase Fixers damage output.

Lets start with the "I can't draw what I want/need!!!"

Now it is true each one of his cards are best in different situations, but that doesn't mean other cards cannot work in the situation they are not best for.

Looking at the tools first, how many of these are super restrictive in their uses? Tire Iron is the only one I can think of, as targets need to be quite low on health for it to work, but tools have the added benefit of returning to hand when playing another, so it may be worth slapping that down when it is needed to get a killing blow, then switching back to the other tool the following turn.

Jack Handle is certainly best when facing tons of targets or when forced to hit heroes. How many villains have very low target count and do not force heroes to hit themself? Spite, that's all. So the majority of the time, it's a pretty good card to keep in play. Sure it may not help every turn, but when the villain makes Fixer try and hit a hero for 2 damage, it's great that he does it to all non-heroes instead.

Dual Crowbars functions a lot like Jack Handle, in two targets are great! But it also has that +1, so even against someone like Spite, you still get a benefit. Even when forced to hit another hero, you get to hit the big bad as well. So once again, never a bad time to play it.

Hoist Chain, it reduces damage a target can deal... I can't see any reason why this would be a bad card to play... I certainly don't hate seeing it in my hand.

Finally Pipe Wrench, +1 damage dealt and -1 damage taken. Good, all around card. Never is painful to have it being the only tool available.

My thought process says Tools are actually quite diverse, with only Tire Iron being very restrictive on when to use it. Jack Handle being a distant second because of Spite. Everything else can be the one in play, even if it's not the best tool for the job.

I am not going to do the same thing with the Styles, as they are the most restrictive between Style and Tools. But that is why they have Meditation. But even so, Gease Monkey Fist or Driving Mantis are never bad to have in play.

Lastly we have Grease Gun, Harmony, Bloody Knuckles, Tool Box, Salvage Yard, Charge, and Overdrive. Salavage Yard is really the only card that is worth holding on to. Harmony should probably be first even without a Style or Tool in play, just so that way when you get both you'll get the bonuses right then. Unless of course you need damage immediately, Bloody Knuckles would typically be first for me, unless I know I am going to be hit a lot. Grease Gun of course saved for just whenever mostly.

I've had games where I had only one card in play, and I still kicked ass because of Bloody Knuckles, Charge, and Overdrive. After all, if I am not drawing Styles and Tools, then I am drawing the great One-Shots or Bloody Knuckles.

If for some reason the opening hand is made up of only Riveting Cranes, Alternating Tiger Claws, Tire Irons, and/or Salvage Yards, play Tire Iron. If Tire Iron is absent, play one of the two Styles. Odd are, the next card will be something worth while. It's only 8 cards in the deck that will most likely have no use at all, if those are the first 8 cards someone draws, then that's some bad shuffling.

 

Now for the grand "I have the Style and Tool I want in play, but now half my deck is dead weight"

This is actually the case for most heroes... Wraith wants to focus on damage, Razor Ordinance, Throwing Knives/Stun Bolt, Utility Belt, and Micro Targeting Computer. What else does she have to do? Play Equipment cards until the villain is killable by a Inventory Barrage... Maybe throw in a Throat Jab or two. Argent Adept gets the Harp, Lyra, a third instrument, Inspiring Supertonic, Counterpoint Bulwark/Inventive Preperation, and possibly a Melody. Then what? Play more songs and instruments just incase he wants to change things up. It's really nothing unique to Fixer, he gets some cards in play, plays his one-shots or Bloody Knuckles on occasion. Most of my games tend to last 4-7 rounds and only 30-45 minutes long. If Fixer does get the combination he was achieving for, the game doesn't really last that long where he gets bummed for not having to switch Styles or Tools. Mainly because of other cards he can play. Sometimes situations can also change quite easily, calling for a new Tool or Style.

 

Also!!!! I should note that I never play Fixer with want a particular combo in play. Every game I play him, I play with what i've got. I've had very few games where I had played Fixer and felt he didn't contribute. I've had no games playing as Fixer were I was bored.

I've used a house rule for vanilla Fixer that worked well for me and doesn't change his core gameplay too much. It's also somewhat similar to his new Darkwatch card.

 

Essentially, replace his Strike ability with:

 

STRIKE - Power: You may discard a card. If you do, Mr. Fixer deals one target 2 melee damage. If you don't, Mr. Fixer deals one target 1 melee damage.

 

The modified Strike works well in conjunction with Fixer's Toolbox, and I've found in playtesting that it helps to make up for those situations where a villain or Environment does something like destroying a bunch of ongoing or equipment cards (you know, that Dual Crowbars you've been trying to draw the whole damn game and just finally put out last round), which usually is murderously devastating to Fixer's flow and makes him annoying as hell to play. Conversely, it's not overpowered because it limits your hand greatly if you rely on it too much.

 

Bloody Knuckles I still feel is one of the worst cards in the game, I've never played it and not regretted it. Though as I've noted before when talking about Fixer and Bloody Knuckles, I also think Smoke Bomb is an annoying card to play simply because you can't destroy it at will and it's well known that Wraith is one of the more useful heroes.

By the time you get both a Tool and Style, Harmony and Salvage Yard will be cards you'll probably want, meaning there are still 18 cards in the his deck that are great.

Bloody Knuckles is only situationally great; there are many cases where the bonus damage you deal is worth less than the HP you'll lose to multiple attacks boosted against you.  Harmony is Limited, Grease Gun prohibits your own strikes, and Salvage Yard might be incredible or useless depending on who your teammates are and what they've been doing.  Overdrive and Charge are the only cards in his deck which are consistently helpful, and by themselves they leave him looking pathetic next to Haka or F6 Wraith.

The luck doesn't seem to be that great, unless your luck is so bad that you constantly get Alternating Tiger Claw, Riveting Crane, Tire Iron, Harmony, and Salavage Yard on the top of the deck, but if that were the case, you could get a Style and Tool in play with Harmony. I do consistently get Riveting Crane or Alternating Tiger Claw, and often Salvage Yard too.  Harmony, not so much, and Tools of any variety almost never.  Without a tool, Harmony is a blank card.  Without a damage buff, Riveting Crane is a blank card.  ATC is only useful against villains with reduction, and you're still just plinking for 1.  If Fixer can't find a Tool, he's pretty much worthless, and he has only 10 in his deck and no way of searching for them.

  An average turn for Ra is about five damage, depending on exactly what he gets; sometimes it's more and sometimes it's less, but his average is close to Fixer's maximum, and Fixer's average is close to Ra's minimum (assuming you're not playing Horus of Two Horizons).

I'm think you may need to start shuffling your decks better, as you seem to draw the same cards quite often.

That is certainly possible.  Dovetail-shuffling SOTM cards is difficult since they're so thick and stiff (otherwise, of course, this is an advantage), so I usually do the overhead-chop method, which probably does tend to leave some clumps of the same cards together for a few games in a row.  Still, most heroes perform well in spite of this possibly deficient randomization.  The Adept doesn't get Arcane Cadence as often as I might like, and often goes without an Instrument for far too long - but he's able to make some contribution, unless his only card in play is Cedistic Dissonant.  Fixer, in most cases, is lucky to be able to deal 2 damage with a card play, when so many heroes can do it without one.

I would say about 40% of my games are H=3, and usually the rest was 35% 4's and 25% 5's, although lately it's strangely reversed.  Advanced games are semi-rare, and I tend to less often choose advanced against DR-using villains because it leads me to forget to account for DR, so I have to redo all my math.  The last game I played against Ambuscade was supposed to be Advanced, but I spaced on the DR for an entire round and retroactively made it a normal game so that I'd played it correctly; the same happened with the Dreamer once.  When DR is on cards, like Gene-Bound Guard, I can remember it, but when it's an Advanced mode that I ignore half the time, I tend to ignore it the other half as well.

My reaction to this is to regard Fixer as a specialist hero, who should be left on the bench unless you're specifically facing a DR villain.  Which is getting perilously close to the likes of a Circle of Protection: Color in Magic.  I have much more respect for cards and decks that function equally well in all circumstances.
